entries.4afb7dca99b548a35f6e6fdbba340156a8630498: <div sID="gen11604" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="66" osisID="Ps.66" sID="Ps.66"/> <div eID="gen11604" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11605" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen11606" type="x-p"/> This is a thanksgiving-psalm, and it is of such a general use and application that we need not suppose it penned upon any particular occasion. All people are here called upon to praise God, I. For the general instances of his sovereign dominion and power in the whole creation, <reference osisRef="Ps.66.1-Ps.66.7">ver. 1-7</reference>. II. For the special tokens of his favour to the church, his peculiar people, <reference osisRef="Ps.66.8-Ps.66.12">ver. 8-12</reference>. And then, III. The psalmist praises God for his own experiences of his goodness to him in particular, especially in answering his prayers, <reference osisRef="Ps.66.13-Ps.66.20">ver. 13-20</reference>. If we have learned in every thing to give thanks for ancient and modern mercies, public and personal mercies, we shall know how to sing this psalm with grace and understanding.
entries.3a3a689dfcba8f70d078ab52c9346b5059dd3998: <div eID="gen11606" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen11605" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">All Mankind Exhorted to Praise God.</title> <div sID="gen11607" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Make a joyful noise unto God, all ye lands: 2 Sing forth the honour of his name: make his praise glorious. <hi type="super">3</hi> Say unto God, How terrible <hi type="italic">art thou in</hi> thy works! through the greatness of thy power shall thine enemies submit themselves unto thee. <hi type="super">4</hi> All the earth shall worship thee, and shall sing unto thee; they shall sing <hi type="italic">to</hi> thy name. Selah. <hi type="super">5</hi> Come and see the works of God: <hi type="italic">he is</hi> terrible <hi type="italic">in his</hi> doing toward the children of men. <hi type="super">6</hi> He turned the sea into dry <hi type="italic">land:</hi> they went through the flood on foot: there did we rejoice in him. <hi type="super">7</hi> He ruleth by his power for ever; his eyes behold the nations: let not the rebellious exalt themselves. Selah. <div eID="gen11607" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11608" type="x-p"/> I. In these verses the psalmist calls upon all people to praise God, <hi type="italic">all lands, all the earth,</hi> all the inhabitants of the world that are capable of praising God, <reference osisRef="Ps.66.1">v. 1</reference>. 1. This speaks the glory of God, that he is worthy to be praised by all, for he is good to all and furnishes every nation with matter for praise. 2. The duty of man, that all are obliged to praise God; it is part of the law of creation, and therefore is required of every creature. 3. A prediction of the conversion of the Gentiles to the faith of Christ; the time should come when all lands should praise God, and this incense should in every place be offered to him. 4. A hearty good-will which the psalmist had to this good work of praising God. He will abound in it himself, and wishes that God might have his tribute paid him by all the nations of the earth and not by the land of Israel only. He excites all lands, (1.) To <hi type="italic">make a joyful noise to God.</hi> Holy joy is that devout affection which should animate all our praises; and, though it is not making a noise in religion that God will accept of (hypocrites are said to <hi type="italic">cause their voice to be heard on high,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.58.4">Isa. lviii. 4</reference>), yet, in praising God, [1.] We must be hearty and zealous, and must do what we do with all our might, with all that is within us. [2.] We must be open and public, as those that are not ashamed of our Master. And both these are implied in making a noise, a joyful noise. (2.) To sing with pleasure, and to <hi type="italic">sing forth,</hi> for the edification of others, <hi type="italic">the honour of his name,</hi> that is, of all that whereby he has made himself known, <reference osisRef="Ps.66.2">v. 2</reference>. That which is the honour of God's name ought to be the matter of our praise. (3.) To <hi type="italic">make his praise glorious</hi> as far as we can. In praising God we must do it so as to glorify him, and that must be the scope and drift of all our praises. <hi type="italic">Reckon it your greatest glory to praise God,</hi> so some. It is the highest honour the creature is capable of to be to the Creator for a name and a praise. <div eID="gen11608" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11609" type="x-p"/> II. He had called upon all lands to praise God (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.1">v. 1</reference>), and he foretels (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.4">v. 4</reference>) that they shall do so: <hi type="italic">All the earth shall worship thee;</hi> some in all parts of the earth, even the remotest regions, for <hi type="italic">the everlasting gospel shall be preached to every nation and kindred;</hi> and this is the purport of it, <hi type="italic">Worship him that made heaven and earth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.14.6-Rev.14.7">Rev. xiv. 6, 7</reference>. Being thus sent forth, it shall not return void, but shall bring all the earth, more or less, to worship God, and sing unto him. In gospel times God shall be worshipped by the singing of Psalms. They shall <hi type="italic">sing to God,</hi> that is, <hi type="italic">sing to his name,</hi> for it is only to his declarative glory, that by which he has made himself known, not to his essential glory, that we can contribute any thing by our praises. <div eID="gen11609" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11610" type="x-p"/> III. That we may be furnished with matter for praise, we are here called upon <hi type="italic">to come and see the works of God;</hi> for <hi type="italic">his own works praise him,</hi> whether we do or no; and the reason why we do not praise him more and better is because we do not duly and attentively observe them. Let us therefore see God's works and observe the instances of his wisdom, power, and faithfulness in them (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.5">v. 5</reference>), and then speak of them, and speak of them to him (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Say unto God, How terrible art thou in thy works, terrible in thy doings!</hi> 1. God's works are wonderful in themselves, and such as, when duly considered, may justly fill us with amazement. God <hi type="italic">is terrible</hi> (that is, admirable) in his works, through the greatness of his power, which is such, and shines so brightly, so strongly, in all he does, that it may be truly said there are <hi type="italic">not any works like unto his works.</hi> Hence he is said to be <hi type="italic">fearful in praises,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.15.11">Exod. xv. 11</reference>. In all his doings towards the children of men he is terrible, and to be eyed with a holy awe. Much of religion lies in a reverence for the divine Providence. 2. They are formidable to his enemies, and have many a time forced and frightened them into a feigned submission (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.3">v. 3</reference>): <hi type="italic">Through the greatness of thy power,</hi> before which none can stand, <hi type="italic">shall thy enemies submit themselves unto thee; they shall lie unto thee</hi> (so the word is), that is, they shall be compelled, sorely against their wills, to make their peace with thee upon any terms. Subjection extorted by fear is seldom sincere, and therefore force is no proper means of propagating religion, nor can there be much joy of such proselytes to the church as will in the end be found liars unto it, <reference osisRef="Deut.33.29">Deut. xxxiii. 29</reference>. 3. They are comfortable and beneficial to his people, <reference osisRef="Ps.66.6">v. 6</reference>. When Israel came out of Egypt, <hi type="italic">he turned the sea into dry land</hi> before them, which encouraged them to follow God's guidance through the wilderness; and, when they were to enter Canaan, for their encouragement in their wars Jordan was divided before them, and <hi type="italic">they went through that flood on foot;</hi> and such foot, so signally owned by heaven, might well pass for cavalry, rather than infantry, in the wars of the Lord. There did the enemies tremble before them (<reference osisRef="Exod.15.14-Exod.15.15">Exod. xv. 14, 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.5.1">Josh. v. 1</reference>), but <hi type="italic">there did we rejoice in him,</hi> both trust his power (for relying on God is often expressed by rejoicing in him) and sing his praise, <reference osisRef="Ps.106.12">Ps. cvi. 12</reference>. There did we rejoice; that is, our ancestors did, and we in their loins. The joys of our fathers were our joys, and we ought to look upon ourselves as sharers in them. 4. They are commanding to all. God by his works keeps up his dominion in the world (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">He rules by his power for ever; his eyes behold the nations.</hi> (1.) God has a commanding eye; from the height of heaven his eye commands all the inhabitants of the world, and he has a clear and full view of them all. <hi type="italic">His eyes run to and fro through the earth;</hi> the most remote and obscure nations are under his inspection. (2.) He has a commanding arm; his power rules, rules for ever, and is never weakened, never obstructed. <hi type="italic">Strong is his hand, and high is his right hand.</hi> Hence he infers, <hi type="italic">Let not the rebellious exalt themselves;</hi> let not those that have revolting and rebellious hearts dare to rise up in any overt acts of rebellion against God, as Adonijah exalted himself, saying, <hi type="italic">I will be king.</hi> Let not those that are in rebellion against God exalt themselves as if there were any probability that they should gain their point. No; let them be still, for God hath said, <hi type="italic">I will be exalted,</hi> and man cannot gainsay it.
entries.945bcba32c73051223116e6096c90ecb31d8e820: <div eID="gen11610" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Saints Exhorted to Praise God.</title> <div sID="gen11611" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> O bless our God, ye people, and make the voice of his praise to be heard: <hi type="super">9</hi> Which holdeth our soul in life, and suffereth not our feet to be moved. <hi type="super">10</hi> For thou, O God, hast proved us: thou hast tried us, as silver is tried. <hi type="super">11</hi> Thou broughtest us into the net; thou laidst affliction upon our loins. <hi type="super">12</hi> Thou hast caused men to ride over our heads; we went through fire and through water: but thou broughtest us out into a wealthy <hi type="italic">place.</hi> <div eID="gen11611" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11612" type="x-p"/> In these verses the psalmist calls upon God's people in a special manner to praise him. Let all lands do it, but Israel's land particularly. Bless our God; bless him as ours, a God in covenant with us, and that takes care of us as his own. Let them <hi type="italic">make the voice of his praise to be heard</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.8">v. 8</reference>); for from whom should it be heard but from those who are his peculiar favourites and select attendants? Two things we have reason to bless God for:— <div eID="gen11612" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11613" type="x-p"/> I. Common protection (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.9">v. 9</reference>): <hi type="italic">He holdeth our soul in life,</hi> that it may not drop away of itself; for, being continually in our hands, it is apt to slip through our fingers. We must own that it is the good providence of God that keeps life and soul together and his visitation that preserves our spirit. <hi type="italic">He puts our soul in life,</hi> so the word is. He that gave us our being, by a constant renewed act upholds us in our being, and his providence is a continued creation. When we are ready to faint and perish he restores our soul, and so puts it, as it were, into a new life, giving new comforts. <hi type="italic">Non est vivere, sed valere, vita—It is not existence, but happiness, that deserves the name of life.</hi> But we are apt to stumble and fall, and are exposed to many destructive accidents, killing disasters as well as killing diseases, and therefore as to these also we are guarded by the divine power. He <hi type="italic">suffers not our feet to be moved,</hi> preventing many unforeseen evils, which we ourselves were not aware of our danger from. To him we owe it that we have not, long ere this, fallen into endless ruin. <hi type="italic">He will keep the feet of his saints.</hi> <div eID="gen11613" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11614" type="x-p"/> II. Special deliverance from great distress. Observe, <div eID="gen11614" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11615" type="x-p"/> 1. How grievous the distress and danger were, <reference osisRef="Ps.66.11-Ps.66.12">v. 11, 12</reference>. What particular trouble of the church this refers to does not appear; it might be the trouble of some private persons or families only. But, whatever it was, they were surprised with it as a bird with a snare, enclosed and entangled in it as a fish in a net; they were pressed down with it, and kept under as with a load <hi type="italic">upon their loins,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.66.11">v. 11</reference>. But they owned the hand of God in it. We are never in the net but God brings us into it, never under affliction but God lays it upon us. Is any thing more dangerous than fire and water? <hi type="italic">We went through both,</hi> that is, afflictions of different kinds; the end of one trouble was the beginning of another; when we had got clear of one sort of dangers we found ourselves involved in dangers of another sort. Such may be the troubles of the best of God's saints, but he has promised, <hi type="italic">When thou passest through the waters, through the fire, I will be with thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.43.1">Isa. xliii. 1</reference>. Yet proud and cruel men may be as dangerous as fire and water, and more so. <hi type="italic">Beware of men,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.10.17">Matt. x. 17</reference>. When men rose up against us, that was fire and water, and all that is threatening (<reference osisRef="Ps.124.2-Ps.124.4">Ps. cxxiv. 2, 3, 4</reference>), and that was the case here: "<hi type="italic">Thou hast caused men to ride over our heads,</hi> to trample upon us and insult over us, to hector and abuse us, nay, and to make perfect slaves of us; they have said to our souls, <hi type="italic">Bow down, that we may go over,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Isa.51.23">Isa. li. 23</reference>. While it is the pleasure of good princes to rule in the hearts of their subjects it is the pride of tyrants to ride over their heads; yet the afflicted church in this also owns the hand of God: "Thou hast caused them thus to abuse us;" for the most furious oppressor has no power but what is given him from above. <div eID="gen11615" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11616" type="x-p"/> 2. How gracious God's design was in bringing them into this distress and danger. See what the meaning of it is (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.10">v. 10</reference>): <hi type="italic">Thou, O God! hast proved us, and tried us.</hi> Then we are likely to get good by our afflictions, when we look upon them under this notion, for then we may see God's grace and love at the bottom of them and our own honour and benefit in the end of them. By afflictions we are proved as silver in the fire. (1.) That our graces, by being tried, may be made more evident and so we may be approved, as silver, when it is touched and marked sterling, and this will be <hi type="italic">to our praise at the appearing of Jesus Christ</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.1.7">1 Pet. i. 7</reference>) and perhaps in this world. Job's integrity and constancy were manifested by his afflictions. (2.) That our graces, by being exercised, may be made more strong and active, and so we may be improved, as silver when it is refined by the fire and made more clear from its dross; and this will be to our unspeakable advantage, for thus we are made partakers of God's holiness, <reference osisRef="Heb.12.10">Heb. xii. 10</reference>. Public troubles are for the purifying of the church, <reference osisRef="Dan.11.35">Dan. xi. 35</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.2.10">Rev. ii. 10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Deut.8.2">Deut. viii. 2</reference>. <div eID="gen11616" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11617" type="x-p"/> 3. How glorious the issue was at last. The troubles of the church will certainly end well; these do so, for (1.) The outlet of the trouble is happy. They are in fire and water, but they get through them: "<hi type="italic">We went through fire and water,</hi> and did not perish in the flames or floods." Whatever the troubles of the saints are, blessed be God, there is a way through them. (2.) The inlet to a better state is much more happy: <hi type="italic">Thou broughtest us out into a wealthy place,</hi> into a <hi type="italic">well-watered</hi> place (so the word is), <hi type="italic">like the gardens of the Lord,</hi> and therefore fruitful. God brings his people into trouble that their comforts afterwards may be the sweeter and that their affliction may thus yield the peaceable fruit of righteousness, which will make the poorest place in the world a wealthy place.
entries.f90eed06bb51ee4622be43a7797cf8d0b94c00ae: <div eID="gen11617" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">David Resolves to Praise God; David Declaring What God Has Done for His Soul.</title> <div sID="gen11618" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> I will go into thy house with burnt offerings: I will pay thee my vows, <hi type="super">14</hi> Which my lips have uttered, and my mouth hath spoken, when I was in trouble. <hi type="super">15</hi> I will offer unto thee burnt sacrifices of fatlings, with the incense of rams; I will offer bullocks with goats. Selah. <hi type="super">16</hi> Come <hi type="italic">and</hi> hear, all ye that fear God, and I will declare what he hath done for my soul. <hi type="super">17</hi> I cried unto him with my mouth, and he was extolled with my tongue. <hi type="super">18</hi> If I regard iniquity in my heart, the Lord will not hear <hi type="italic">me:</hi> <hi type="super">19</hi> <hi type="italic">But</hi> verily God hath heard <hi type="italic">me;</hi> he hath attended to the voice of my prayer. <hi type="super">20</hi> Blessed <hi type="italic">be</hi> God, which hath not turned away my prayer, nor his mercy from me. <div eID="gen11618" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11619" type="x-p"/> The psalmist, having before stirred up all people, and all God's people in particular, to bless the Lord, here stirs up himself and engages himself to do it. <div eID="gen11619" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11620" type="x-p"/> I. In his devotions to his God, <reference osisRef="Ps.66.13-Ps.66.15">v. 13-15</reference>. He had called upon others to sing God's praises and to make a joyful noise with them; but, for himself, his resolutions go further, and he will praise God, 1. By costly sacrifices, which, under the law, were offered to the honour of God. All people had not wherewithal to offer these sacrifices, or wanted zeal to be at such an expense in praising God; but David, for his part, being able, is as willing, in this chargeable way to pay his homage to God (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.13">v. 13</reference>): <hi type="italic">I will go into thy house with burnt-offerings.</hi> His sacrifices should be public, in the place which God had chosen: "I will go into thy house with them." Christ is our temple, to whom we must bring our spiritual gifts, and by whom they are sanctified. They should be the best of the king—<hi type="italic">burnt-sacrifices,</hi> which were wholly consumed upon the altar, to the honour of God, and of which the offerer had no share; and burnt-sacrifices <hi type="italic">of fatlings,</hi> not the lame or the lean, but the best fed, and such as would be most acceptable at his own table. God, who is the best, must be served with the best we have. The feast God makes for us is a <hi type="italic">feast of fat things, full of marrow</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.25.6">Isa. xxv. 6</reference>), and such sacrifices should we bring to him. He will <hi type="italic">offer bullocks with goats,</hi> so liberal will he be in his return of praise, and not strait-handed: he would not offer that which cost him nothing, but that which cost him a great deal. And this <hi type="italic">with the incense of rams,</hi> that is, with the fat of rams, which being burnt upon the altar, the smoke of it would ascend like the smoke of incense. Or <hi type="italic">rams with incense.</hi> The incense typifies Christ's intercession, without which the fattest of our sacrifices will not be accepted. 2. By a conscientious performance of his vows. We do not acceptably praise God for our deliverance out of trouble unless we make conscience of paying the vows we made when we were in trouble. This was the psalmist's resolution (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.13-Ps.66.14">v. 13, 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">I will pay thee my vows, which my lips have uttered when I was in trouble.</hi> Note, (1.) It is very common, and very commendable, when we are under the pressure of any affliction, or in the pursuit of any mercy, to make vows, and solemnly to speak them before the Lord, to bind ourselves out from sin and bind ourselves more closely to our duty; not as if this were an equivalent, or valuable consideration, for the favour of God, but a qualification for receiving the tokens of that favour. (2.) The vows which we made when we were in trouble must not be forgotten when the trouble is over, but be carefully performed, for better it is not to vow than to vow and not pay. <div eID="gen11620" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen11621" type="x-p"/> II. In his declarations to his friends, <reference osisRef="Ps.66.16">v. 16</reference>. He calls together a congregation of good people to hear his thankful narrative of God's favours to him: "<hi type="italic">Come and hear, all you that fear God,</hi> for, 1. You will join with me in my praises and help me in giving thanks." And we should be as desirous of the assistance of those that fear God in returning thanks for the mercies we have received as in praying for those we want. 2. "You will be edified and encouraged by that which I have to say. <hi type="italic">The humble shall hear of it and be glad,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.34.2">Ps. xxxiv. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">Those that fear thee will be glad when they see me</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.74">Ps. cxix. 74</reference>), and therefore let me have their company, and I will declare to them, not to vain carnal people that will banter it and make a jest of it" (pearls are not to be cast before swine); "but to those that fear God, and will make a good use of it, I will declare what God has done for my soul," not in pride and vain-glory, that he might be thought more a favourite of heaven than other people, but for the honour of God, to which we owe this as a just debt, and for the edification of others. Note, God's people should communicate their experiences to each other. We should take all occasions to tell one another of the great and kind things which God has done for us, especially which he has done for our souls, the spiritual blessings with which he has blessed us in heavenly things; these we should be most affected with ourselves, and therefore with these we should be desirous to affect others. Now what was it that God had done for his soul? (1.) He had wrought in him a love to the duty of prayer, and had by his grace enlarged his heart in that duty (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.17">v. 17</reference>): <hi type="italic">I cried unto him with my mouth.</hi> But if God, among other things done for our souls, had not given us the Spirit of adoption, teaching and enabling us to cry, <hi type="italic">Abba, Father,</hi> we should never have done it. That God has given us leave to pray, a command to pray, encouragements to pray, and (to crown all) a heart to pray, is what we have reason to mention with thankfulness to his praise; and the more if, when we cried to him with our mouth, <hi type="italic">he was extolled with our tongue,</hi> that is, if we were enabled by faith and hope to give glory to him when we were seeking for mercy and grace from him, and to praise him for mercy in prospect though not yet in possession. By crying to him we do indeed extol him. He is pleased to reckon himself honoured by the humble believing prayers of the upright, and this is a great thing which he has done for our souls, that he has been pleased so far to unite interests with us that, in seeking our own welfare, we seek his glory. <hi type="italic">His exaltation was under my tongue</hi> (so it may be read); that is, I was considering in my mind how I might exalt and magnify his name. When prayers are in our mouths praises must be in our hearts. (2.) He had wrought in him a dread of sin as an enemy to prayer (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.18">v. 18</reference>): <hi type="italic">If I regard iniquity in my heart,</hi> I know very well <hi type="italic">the Lord will not hear me.</hi> The Jewish writers, some of them that have the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy, put a very corrupt gloss upon these words: <hi type="italic">If I regard iniquity in my heart,</hi> that is (say they), If I allow myself only in heart-sins, and iniquity does not break out in my words and actions, <hi type="italic">God will not hear me,</hi> that is, he will not be offended with me, will take no notice of it, so as to lay it to my charge; as if heart-sins were no sins in God's account. The falsehood of this our Saviour has shown in his spiritual exposition of the law, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.7-Matt.5.48">Matt. v.</reference> But the sense of this place is plain: <hi type="italic">If I regard iniquity in my heart,</hi> that is, "If I have favourable thoughts of it, if I love it, indulge it, and allow myself in it, if I treat it as a friend and bid it welcome, make provision for it and am loth to part with it, if I roll it under my tongue as a sweet morsel, though it be but a heart sin that is thus countenanced and made much of, if I delight in it after the inward man, God will not hear my prayer, will not accept it, nor be pleased with it, nor can I expect an answer of peace to it." Note, Iniquity, regarded in the heart, will certainly spoil the comfort and success of prayer; for <hi type="italic">the sacrifice of the wicked is an abomination to the Lord.</hi> Those that continue in love and league with sin have no interest either in the promise or in the Mediator, and therefore cannot expect to speed in prayer. (3.) He had graciously granted him an answer of peace to his prayers (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.19">v. 19</reference>): "<hi type="italic">But verily God has heard me;</hi> though, being conscious to myself of much amiss in me, I began to fear that my prayers would be rejected, yet, to my comfort, I found that God was pleased to regard them." This God did for his soul, by answering his prayer, he gave him a token of his favour and an evidence that he had wrought a good work in him. And therefore he concludes (<reference osisRef="Ps.66.20">v. 20</reference>), <hi type="italic">Blessed be God.</hi> The <reference osisRef="Ps.66.18-Ps.66.19">two foregoing verses</reference> are the major and minor propositions of a syllogism: <hi type="italic">If I regard iniquity in my heart, God will not hear my prayer;</hi> that is the proposition: <hi type="italic">but verily God has heard me;</hi> that is the assumption, from which he might have rationally inferred, "Therefore I do not regard iniquity in my heart;" but, instead of taking the comfort to himself, he gives the praise to God: <hi type="italic">Blessed be God.</hi> Whatever are the premises, God's glory must always be the conclusion. <hi type="italic">God has heard me,</hi> and therefore <hi type="italic">blessed be God.</hi> Note, What we win by prayer we must wear with praise. Mercies in answer to prayer do, in a special manner, oblige us to be thankful. He has <hi type="italic">not turned away my prayer, nor his mercy.</hi> Lest it should be thought that the deliverance was granted for the sake of some worthiness in his prayer, he ascribes it to God's mercy. This he adds by way of correction: "It was not my prayer that fetched the deliverance, but his mercy that sent it." <hi type="italic">Therefore</hi> God does not turn away our prayer, because he does not turn away his own mercy, for that is the foundation of our hopes and the fountain of our comforts, and therefore ought to be the matter of our praises.  <chapter eID="Ps.66"/> <div eID="gen11621" type="x-p"/>

entries.3effaaf74f8203d44f1eaf01e30ec7e585c7aaf9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6207"/><title type="x-s2">PSALM 66</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Ps.66.1-Ps.66.20">Psa 66:1-20</reference>. The writer invites all men to unite in praise, cites some striking occasions for it, promises special acts of thanksgiving, and celebrates God's great mercy.</title> <div sID="gen9492" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6207"/><hi type="bold">1. Make ... noise--</hi>or, "Shout." <div eID="gen9492" type="x-p"/>
entries.a7fa1457d2440f699c446c773c203d5e029a5ba0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6208"/><div sID="gen9493" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6208"/><hi type="bold">2. his name--</hi>as in <reference osisRef="Ps.29.2">Psa 29:2</reference>.<div eID="gen9493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9494" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">make his praise glorious--</hi>literally, "place honor, His praise," or, "as to His praise"; that is, let His praise be such as will glorify Him, or, be honorable to Him. <div eID="gen9494" type="x-p"/>
entries.282ae8e3ae3d9e1addf9609adef3366d263e64ff: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6209"/><div sID="gen9495" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6209"/>3-4. A specimen of the praise.<div eID="gen9495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9496" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">How terrible--</hi>(Compare <reference osisRef="Ps.65.8">Psa 65:8</reference>).<div eID="gen9496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9497" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">submit--</hi>(Compare Margin), show a forced subjection (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.44">Psa 18:44</reference>), produced by terror. <div eID="gen9497" type="x-p"/>
entries.36700556453eea7a8c71839c8f15c2c11d583c0a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6210"/><div sID="gen9498" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6210"/>5-6. The terrible works illustrated in Israel's history (<reference osisRef="Exod.14.21">Ex 14:21</reference>). By this example let rebels be admonished. <div eID="gen9498" type="x-p"/>
entries.d73a0dabf6642eb5c651cc7e6ebb00bc62ed89d7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6211"/><div sID="gen9499" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6211"/><hi type="bold">7. behold the nations--</hi>watch their conduct. <div eID="gen9499" type="x-p"/>
entries.0f45e68692ee7cacdf1e5d94bf5d842aa2fd0663: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6212"/><div sID="gen9500" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6212"/>8-9. Here is, perhaps, cited a case of recent deliverance. <div eID="gen9500" type="x-p"/>
entries.ff7c43fd76b690737459dc3458283c1c4bbcf1b3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6214"/><div sID="gen9503" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6214"/>10-12. Out of severe trials, God had brought them to safety (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.48.10">Is 48:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.7">1Pe 1:7</reference>). <div eID="gen9503" type="x-p"/>
entries.f64bf922f0a9065f43915085141db829c27de5c5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6217"/><div sID="gen9509" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6217"/>13-15. These full and varied offerings constitute the payment of vows (<reference osisRef="Lev.22.18-Lev.22.23">Le 22:18-23</reference>). <div eID="gen9509" type="x-p"/>
entries.ef2d2194bd780aa87553ffd8525b09e089b2ad2d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv6219"/><div sID="gen9512" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv6219"/>16-20. With these he unites his public thanks, inviting those who fear God (<reference osisRef="Ps.60.4">Psa 60:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.61.5">61:5</reference>, His true worshippers) to hear. He vindicates his sincerity, inasmuch as God would not hear hypocrites, but had heard him. <div eID="gen9512" type="x-p"/>

entries.5b1b33424074295896ff01756296a2ab5825636c: <div eID="gen20710" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen20711" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20712" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20712" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen20711" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen20713" type="x-p"/> The psalmist exhorts all to praise God for the wonders he has wrought, <reference osisRef="Psa.66.1-Psa.66.4">Psa 66:1-4</reference>; calls on Israel to consider his mighty acts in behalf of their fathers, <reference osisRef="Psa.66.5-Psa.66.7">Psa 66:5-7</reference>; his goodness in their own behalf <reference osisRef="Psa.66.8-Psa.66.12">Psa 66:8-12</reference>; he resolves to pay his vows to God, and offer his promised sacrifices, <reference osisRef="Psa.66.13-Psa.66.15">Psa 66:13-15</reference>; calls on all to hear what God had done for his soul, <reference osisRef="Psa.66.15-Psa.66.20">Psa 66:15-20</reference>. <div eID="gen20713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20714" type="x-p"/> There is nothing particular in the title of the Psalm. It is not attributed to David either by the Hebrew, Chaldee, Syriac, Septuagint, Vulgate, or Ethiopic. The Arabic alone prefixes the name of David. The Vulgate, Septuagint, Ethiopic, and Arabic, call it a psalm of the resurrection: but for this there is no authority. By many of the ancients it is supposed to be a celebration of the restoration from the Babylonish captivity. Others think it commemorates the deliverance of Israel from Egypt, their introduction into the Promised Land, and the establishment of the worship of God in Jerusalem. <div eID="gen20714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20715" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen20715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20716" type="x-p"/> Make a joyfull noise - Sing aloud to God, all ye lands - all ye people who, from different parts of the Babylonish empire, are now on return to your own land.
entries.92f6967530503764fa18667b6e7a5c7bfb8da224: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen20716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20717" type="x-p"/> The honor of his name - Let his glorious and merciful acts be the subject of your songs.
entries.37c3444eb16c25513d495b194d55b186e1c72af6: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen20717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20718" type="x-p"/> How terrible art thou - Consider the plagues with which he afflicted Egypt before he brought your fathers from their captivity, which obliged all his enemies to submit. <div eID="gen20718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20719" type="x-p"/> Thine enemies submit themselves - Literally, lie unto thee. This was remarkably the case with Pharaoh and the Egyptians. They promised again and again to let the people go, when the hand of the Lord was upon them: and they as frequently falsified their word.
entries.712b0e8bb90b6fd80bad0d937173bea819b0f136: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen20719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20720" type="x-p"/> All the earth - The whole land shall worship thee. There shall no more an idol be found among the tribes of Israel. This was iterally true. After the Babylonish captivity the Israelites never relapsed into idolatry. <div eID="gen20720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20721" type="x-p"/> Selah - Remark it: this is a well attested truth.
entries.fdef603d04e3afff7109c124b74f39413a5986a7: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen20721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20722" type="x-p"/> Come and see the works of God - Let every man lay God's wonderful dealings with us to heart; and compare our deliverance from Babylon to that of our fathers from Egypt.
entries.ffeabb3830ff79aa02a02f36945fd0c88cb15ef5: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen20722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20723" type="x-p"/> He turned the sea into dry land - This was a plain miracle: no human art or contrivance could do this. Even in the bed of the waters They did rejoice in him. We have not less cause to praise and be thankful.
entries.2fecd722e2e31b0bbdb22433214ab4327c1b4e8b: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen20723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20724" type="x-p"/> Be ruleth by his power - His omnipotence is employed to support his followers, and cast down his enemies. <div eID="gen20724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20725" type="x-p"/> His eyes behold the nations - He sees what they purpose, what they intend to do; and what they will do, if he restrain them not. <div eID="gen20725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20726" type="x-p"/> Let not the rebellious exalt themselves - They shall not succeed in their designs: they have their own aggrandizement in view, but thou wilt disappoint and cast them down. <div eID="gen20726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20727" type="x-p"/> Selah - Mark this. It is true.
entries.30368fe957b06303e04b0b9a5bc0e200fc58ff1c: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen20727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20728" type="x-p"/> O bless our God - Who have so much cause as you to sing praises to the Lord? Hear what he has done for you:
entries.7193e7102b90934fdc49141b769765f519db9db7: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen20728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20729" type="x-p"/> Which holdeth our soul in life - Literally, "he who placeth our soul בחיים bachaiyim, in lives." We are preserved alive, have health of body, and feel the life of God in our hearts. <div eID="gen20729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20730" type="x-p"/> And suffereth not her feet to be moved - Keeps us steadfast in his testimonies. We have our life, our liberty, and our religion. O, what hath the Lord wrought for us! "Make, therefore, the voice of his praise to be heard." Let God and man know you are thankful.
entries.792829dfcbccb3a324ee6961705b24c5e7a93b6f: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen20730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20731" type="x-p"/> For thou, O God, hast proved us - This is a metaphor taken from melting and refining metals; afflictions and trials of various kinds are represented as a furnace where ore is melted, and a crucible where it is refined. And this metaphor is used especially to represent cases where there is doubt concerning the purity of the metal, the quantity of alloy, or even the nature or kind of metal subjected to the trial. So God is said to try the Israelites that he might know what was in them; and whether they would keep his testimonies: and then, according to the issue, his conduct towards them would appear to be founded on reason and justice.
entries.bb67cfb1a91d2afb222f3389f72395cad39f2f85: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen20731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20732" type="x-p"/> Thou broughtest us into the net - This refers well to the case of the Israelites, when, in their departure from Egypt, pursued by the Egyptians, having the Red Sea before them, and no method of escape, Pharaoh said, "The wilderness hath shut them in, - they are entangled;" comparing their state to that of a wild beast in a net. <div eID="gen20732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20733" type="x-p"/> Affliction upon our loins - Perhaps this alludes to that sharp pain in the back and loins which is generally felt on the apprehension of sudden and destructive danger.
entries.141b79ff1c70abc9d94bc3090ef3c16efc195be5: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen20733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20734" type="x-p"/> Thou hast caused men to ride over our heads - Thou hast permitted us to fall under the dominion of our enemies; who have treated us as broken infantry are when the cavalry dashes among their disordered ranks, treading all under the horses' feet. <div eID="gen20734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20735" type="x-p"/> We went through fire and through water - Through afflictions of the most torturing and overwhelming nature. To represent such, the metaphors of fire and water are often used in Scripture. The old Psalter considers these trials as a proof of the uprightness of those who were tried - We passid thrugh fire and watir: that is, thurgh wa and wele, as a man that leves noght his waye for hete na for kald, for dry na for wette; and thou out lede us fra tribulacyon intill koling (cooling) that is, in till endles riste, that we hope to hafe after this travell. <div eID="gen20735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20736" type="x-p"/> Wealthy place - Well watered place, to wit, the land of Judea.
entries.cd51d3768ff6a7c0ce1a7030b52ad27a0f30f8b5: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen20736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20737" type="x-p"/> I will go into thy house with burnt-offerings - Now that thou hast restored us to our own land, and established us in it, we will establish thy worship, and offer all the various kinds of sacrifices required by thy law. <div eID="gen20737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20738" type="x-p"/> I will pay thee my vows - We often vowed, if thou wouldst deliver us from our bondage, to worship and serve thee alone: now thou hast heard our prayers, and hast delivered us; therefore will we fulfill our engagements to thee. The old Psalter gives this a pious turn: - I sall yelde till the my woues, that is, the vowes of louying (praising) the; whilk vowes my lipes divisid sayand, that I am noght, and thou arte all: and I hafe nede of the, noght thou of me. This is a right distinction - It is certainly a good distinction, and it is strictly true. The allsufficient God needs not his creatures.
entries.a4dc389f73cb0e6203b9df680e9bbec1c8436ebe: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen20738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20739" type="x-p"/> When I was in trouble - This is generally the time when good resolutions are formed, and vows made; but how often are these forgotten when affliction and calamity are removed!
entries.e0262d022fd9a3865ba52ddd7b483afe8938bf66: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen20739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20740" type="x-p"/> I will offer, etc. - Thou shalt have the best of the herd and of the fold; the lame and the blind shall never be given to thee for sacrifice. <div eID="gen20740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20741" type="x-p"/> The incense of rams - The fine effluvia arising from the burning of the pure fat.
entries.668b630d32d09ab1aa05675cb3c45dcb78097137: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen20741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20742" type="x-p"/> Come and hear, all ye that fear God - While in captivity, the psalmist had sought the Lord with frequent prayer for his own personal salvation, and for the deliverance of the people; and God blessed him, heard his prayer, and turned the captivity. Now that he is returned in safety, he is determined to perform his vows to the Lord; and calls on all them that fear their Maker, who have any religious reverence for him, to attend to his account of the Lord's gracious dealings with him. He proposes to tell them his spiritual experience, what he needed, what he earnestly prayed for, and what God has done for him. Thus he intended to teach them by example, more powerful always than precept, however weighty in itself, and impressively delivered.
entries.87693777752a42a164bc7be8d496541f25de9a81: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen20742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20743" type="x-p"/> I cried unto him with my mouth - My prayer was fervent; he heard and answered; and my tongue celebrated his mercies; and he as graciously received my thanksgiving, as he compassionately heard my prayer.
entries.0bfe4445fa865775a3aca5ab9ec6dcf964a4a76f: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen20743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20744" type="x-p"/> If I regard iniquity in my heart - "If I have seen (ראיתי raithi) iniquity in my heart," if I have known it was there, and encouraged it; if I pretended to be what I was not; if I loved iniquity, while I professed to pray and be sorry for my sin; the Lord, אדני Adonai, my Prop, Stay, and Supporter, would not have heard, and I should have been left without help or support.
entries.7d5b4f07e37d3a67294b2cccf92d0a557e9861a6: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen20744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20745" type="x-p"/> Verily God hath heard me - A sure proof that my prayer was upright, and my heart honest, before him.
entries.6e4878c0dc1d4f5cd94be66eb29ccef507d80da9: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen20745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen20746" type="x-p"/> Blessed be God - I therefore praise God, who has not turned aside my prayer, and who has not withheld his mercy from me. Thus he told them what God had done for his soul.  <chapter eID="Ps.66"/> <div eID="gen20746" type="x-p"/>

entries.b578363b38de91ed33114570abd3f6ac16a046c5: <reference osisRef="Ps.66.1-Ps.66.4">Psa 66:1-4</reference> <div eID="gen9647" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9648" type="x-p"/> The phrase שׂים כבוד ל signifies “to give glory to God” in other passages (<reference osisRef="Josh.7.19">Jos 7:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.42.12">Isa 42:12</reference>), here with a second accusative, either (1) if we take תּהלּתו as an accusative of the object: <hi type="italic">facite laudationem ejus gloriam</hi> = <hi type="italic">gloriosam</hi> (Maurer and others), or (2) if we take כבוד as an accusative of the object and the former word as an accusative of the predicate: <hi type="italic">reddite honorem laudem ejus </hi>(Hengstenberg), or (3) also by taking תהלתו as an apposition: <hi type="italic">reddite honorem, scil. laudem ejus</hi> (Hupfeld). We prefer the middle rendering: give glory as His praise, i.e., to Him as or for praise. It is unnecessary, with Hengstenberg, to render: How terrible art Thou in Thy works! in that case אתּה ought not to be wanting. מעשׂיך might more readily be singular (Hupfeld, Hitzig); but these forms with the softened <hi type="italic">Jod</hi> of the root dwindle down to only a few instances upon closer consideration. The singular of the predicate (what a terrible affair) here, as frequently, e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.119.137">Psa 119:137</reference>, precedes the plural designating things. The song into which the Psalmist here bids the nations break forth, is essentially one with the song of the heavenly harpers in Rev 15:3., which begins, Μεγάλα καὶ θαυμαστὰ τὰ ἔργα σου.
entries.a0e8354c2acc33bce8745c329151935bbe99905e: <reference osisRef="Ps.66.5-Ps.66.7">Psa 66:5-7</reference> <div eID="gen9648" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9649" type="x-p"/> Although the summons: Come and see... (borrowed apparently from <reference osisRef="Ps.46.9">Psa 46:9</reference>), is called forth by contemporary manifestations of God’s power, the consequences of which now lie open to view, the rendering of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.66.6">Psa 66:6</reference></hi>, “then will we rejoice in Him,” is nevertheless unnatural, and, rightly looked at, neither grammar nor the matter requires it. For since שׁם in this passage is equivalent to אז, and the future after אז takes the signification of an aorist; and since the cohortative form of the future can also (e.g., after עד, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.7">Psa 73:7</reference>, and in clauses having a hypothetical sense) be referred to the past, and does sometimes at least occur where the writer throws himself back into the past (<reference osisRef="2Sam.22.38">2Sa 22:38</reference>), the rendering: Then did we rejoice in Him, cannot be assailed on syntactical grounds. On the “we,” cf. <reference osisRef="Josh.5.1">Jos 5:1</reference>, <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi>, Hos 12:1-14 :54. The church of all ages is a unity, the separate parts being jointly involved in the whole. The church here directs the attention of all the world to the mighty deeds of God at the time of the deliverance from Egypt, viz., the laying of the Red Sea and of Jordan dry, inasmuch as it can say in <reference osisRef="Ps.66.7">Psa 66:7</reference>, by reason of that which it has experienced ibn the present, that the sovereign power of God is ever the same: its God rules in His victorious might עולם, i.e., not “over the world,” because that ought to be בּעולם, but “in eternity” (accusative of duration, as in Psa 89:2., <reference osisRef="Ps.45.7">Psa 45:7</reference>), and therefore, as in the former days, so also in all time to come. His eyes keep searching watch among the peoples; the rebellious, who struggle agaisnt His yoke and persecute His people, had better not rise, it may go ill with them. The <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi> runs ירימוּ, for which the <hi type="italic">Kerî</hi> is ירוּמוּ. The meaning remains the same; הרים can (even without יד, ראשׁ, קרן, <reference osisRef="Ps.65.5">Psa 65:5</reference>) mean “to practise exaltation,” <hi type="italic">superbire</hi>. By means of למו this proud bearing is designated as being egotistical, and as unrestrainedly boastful. Only let them not imagine themselves secure in their arrogance! There is One more exalted, whose eye nothing escapes, and to whose irresistible might whatever is not conformed to His gracious will succumbs.
entries.b4022960f60f463eaa441088dc00ccd6ba19dee8: <reference osisRef="Ps.66.8-Ps.66.12">Psa 66:8-12</reference> <div eID="gen9649" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9650" type="x-p"/> The character of the event by which the truth has been verified that the God who redeemed Israel out of Egypt still ever possesses and exercises to the full His ancient sovereign power, is seen from this reiterated call to the peoples to share in Israel’s <hi type="italic">Gloria</hi>. God has averted the peril of death and overthrow from His people: He has put their soul in life (בּחיּים, like בּישׁע in <reference osisRef="Ps.12.6">Psa 12:6</reference>), i.e., in the realm of life; He has not abandoned their foot to tottering unto overthrow (mowT the substantive, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.121.3">Psa 121:3</reference>; cf. the reversed construction in <reference osisRef="Ps.55.23">Psa 55:23</reference>). For God has cast His people as it were into a smelting-furnace or fining-pot in order to purify and to prove them by suffering; - this is a favourite figure with Isaiah and Jeremiah, but is also found in Zec 13:9; Mal 3:3. <reference osisRef="Ezek.19.9">Eze 19:9</reference> is decisive concerning the meaning of מצוּדה, where הביא במצודות signifies “to bring into the holds or prisons;” besides, the figure of the fowling-net (although this is also called מצוּדה as well as מצודה) has no footing here in the context. מצוּדה (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.18.3">Psa 18:3</reference>) signifies <hi type="italic">specula</hi>, and that both a natural and an artificial watch-post on a mountain; here it is the mountain-hold or prison of the enemy, as a figure of the total loss of freedom. The laying on of a heavy burden mentioned by the side of it in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Ps.66.11">Psa 66:11</reference></hi> also accords well with this. מוּעקה, a being oppressed, the pressure of a burden, is a <hi type="italic">Hophal</hi> formation, like מטּה, a being spread out, <reference osisRef="Isa.8.8">Isa 8:8</reference>; cf. the similar masculine forms in <reference osisRef="Ps.69.3">Psa 69:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.8.13">Isa 8:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.14.6">Isa 14:6</reference>; Isa 29:3. The loins are mentioned because when carrying heavy loads, which one has to stoop down in order to take up, the lower spinal region is called into exercise. אנושׁ is frequently (Psa 9:20., <reference osisRef="Ps.10.18">Psa 10:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.56.2">Psa 56:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.51.12">Isa 51:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.10">2Ch 14:10</reference>) the word used for tyrants as being wretched mortals, perishable creatures, in contrast with their all the more revolting, imperious, and self-deified demeanour. God so ordered it, that “wretched men” rode upon Israel’s head. Or is it to be interpreted: He caused them to pass over Israel (cf. <reference osisRef="Ps.129.3">Psa 129:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.51.23">Isa 51:23</reference>)? It can scarcely mean this, since it would then be <hi type="italic">in dorso nostro</hi>, which the Latin versions capriciously substitute. The preposition ל instead of על is used with reference to the phrase ישׁב ל: sitting upon Israel’s head, God caused them to ride along, so that Israel was not able to raise its head freely, but was most ignominiously wounded in its self-esteem. Fire and water are, as in <reference osisRef="Isa.43.2">Isa 43:2</reference>, a figure of vicissitudes and perils of the most extreme character. Israel was nigh to being burnt up and drowned, but God led it forth לרויה, to an abundant fulness, to abundance and superabundance of prosperity. The lxx, which renders εἰς ἀναψυχήν (Jerome absolutely: <hi type="italic">in refrigerium</hi>), has read לרוחה; Symmachus, εἰς εὐρυχωρίαν, probably reading לרחבה (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.45">Psa 119:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.18.20">Psa 18:20</reference>). Both give a stronger antithesis. But the state of straitness or oppression was indeed also a state of privation.
entries.509d29535808fe9d53c7ea40fbdcaa9623299d37: <reference osisRef="Ps.66.13-Ps.66.15">Psa 66:13-15</reference> <div eID="gen9650" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9651" type="x-p"/> From this point onwards the poet himself speaks, but, as the diversity and the kind of the sacrifices show, as being a member of the community at large. The עולות stand first, the girts of adoring homage; בּ is the <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> of the accompaniment, as in <reference osisRef="Lev.16.3">Lev 16:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.1.24">1Sa 1:24</reference>, cf. Heb 9:25. “My vows” refer more especially to פּצה פּה ׃שׁלמי נדר also occurs elsewhere of the involuntary vowing to do extraordinary things urged from one by great distress (Jdg 11:35). אשׁר is an accusative of the object relating to the vows, <hi type="italic">quae aperuerunt</hi> = <hi type="italic">aperiendo nuncupaverunt labia mea</hi> (Geier). In <reference osisRef="Ps.66.15">Psa 66:15</reference> עשׂה, used directly (like the Aramaic and Phoenician עבד) in the signification “to sacrifice” (<reference osisRef="Exod.29.36-Exod.29.41">Exo 29:36-41</reference>, and frequently), alternates with העלה, the synonym of הקטיר. The sacrifices to be presented are enumerated. מיחים (incorrect for מחים) are marrowy, fat lambs; lambs and bullocks (בּקר) have the most universal appropriation among the animals that were fit for sacrifices. The ram (איל), on the contrary, is the animal for the whole burnt-offering of the high priest, of the princes of the tribes, and of the people; and appears also as the animal for the shelamim only in connection with the shelamim of Aaron, of the people, of the princes of the tribes, and, in Num 6:14, of the Nazarite. The younger he-goat (עתּוּד) is never mentioned as an animal for the whole burnt-offering; but, indeed, as an animal for the shelamim of the princes of the tribes in Num. 7. It is, therefore, probable that the shelamim which were to be offered in close connection with the whole burnt-offerings are introduced by עם, so that קטרת signifies the fat portions of the shelamim upon the altar smoking in the fire. The mention of “rams” renders it necessary that we should regard the poet as here comprehending himself among the people when he speaks thus.
entries.3674db6dfa5f6046f861c11decf0c3b756601200: <reference osisRef="Ps.66.16-Ps.66.20">Psa 66:16-20</reference> <div eID="gen9651" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen9652" type="x-p"/> The words in <reference osisRef="Ps.66.16">Psa 66:16</reference> are addressed in the widest extent, as in <reference osisRef="Ps.66.5">Psa 66:5</reference> and <reference osisRef="Ps.66.2">Psa 66:2</reference>, to all who fear God, wheresoever such are to be found on the face of the earth. To all these, for the glory of God and for their own profit, he would gladly relate what God has made him to experience. The individual-looking expression לנפשׁי is not opposed to the fact of the occurrence of a marvellous answering of prayer, to which he refers, being one which has been experienced by him in common with the whole congregation. He cried unto God with his mouth (that is to say, not merely silently in spirit, but audibly and importunately), and a hymn (רומם,<note placement="foot">Kimchi (Michlol 146 <hi type="italic">a</hi>) and Parchon (under רמם) read רומם with <hi type="italic">Pathach</hi>; and Heidenheim and Baer have adopted it.</note> something that rises, collateral form to רומם, as עולל and שׁובב to עולל and שׁובב) was under my tongue; i.e., I became also at once so sure of my being heard, that I even had the song of praise in readiness (vid., <reference osisRef="Ps.10.7">Psa 10:7</reference>), with which I had determined to break forth when the help for which I had prayed, and which was assured to me, should arrive. For the purpose of his heart was not at any time, in contradiction to his words, און, God-abhorred vileness or worthlessness; ראה with the accusative, as in <reference osisRef="Gen.20.10">Gen 20:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.37.37">Psa 37:37</reference> : to aim at, or design anything, to have it in one’s eye. We render: If I had aimed at evil in my heart, the Lord would not hear; not: He would not have heard, but: He would not on any occasion hear. For a hypocritical prayer, coming from a heart which has not its aim sincerely directed towards Him, He does not hear. The idea that such a heart was not hidden behind his prayer is refuted in <reference osisRef="Ps.66.19">Psa 66:19</reference> from the result, which is of a totally opposite character. In the closing doxology the accentuation rightly takes תּפלּתי וחסדּו as belonging together. Prayer and mercy stand in the relation to one another of call and echo. When God turns away from a man his prayer and His mercy, He commands him to be silent and refuses him a favourable answer. The poet, however, praises God that He has deprived him neither of the joyfulness of prayer nor the proof of His favour. In this sense Augustine makes the following practical observation on this passage: <hi type="italic">Cum videris non a te amotam deprecationem tuam, securus esto, quia non est a te amota misericordia ejus.</hi>  <chapter eID="Ps.66"/> <div eID="gen9652" type="x-p"/>

PSALM 66
There may have been one deliverance in particular, which the Psalmist celebrates here in the name of the Church, but he includes the many and various mercies which God had all along conferred upon his chosen people. While he takes notice of the divine interposition in their behalf, in a crisis of great mercy and distress, he suggests it as matter of comfort under trial, that their subjection to the tyranny of their enemies had been designed to prove them as silver in the furnace. At the close, he would appear to speak of himself individually, and adduces it as a proof of his integrity, that God had heard him, for God does not grant acceptance to the wicked.
To the chief musician, the Song of a Psalm.
“This psalm is anonymous; nor can we, with certainty, determine to what time it relates. Venema refers it to the reign of Hezekiah, and supposes it to celebrate the deliverance which was effected by the destruction of Sennacherib’s army. Rudinger is of opinion, that it celebrates the opening of the sacred temple, after the return from Babylon. It must be owned, that we have nothing but conjecture to offer on this subject; yet it appears to me that the latter of these opinions is the most probable.” — Walford.
Psalm 66:1-4
1. Shout unto God, all the earth. 2. Sing the honor of his name: make glorious his praise.
“Ou, mettez gloire a sa louan.” — Fr. marg. “Or, put glory to his praise.”
3. Say unto God, How terrible art thou in thy works! in the greatness of thy power shall thine enemies lie [or feign submission] unto thee. 4. All the earth shall worship thee, and they shall sing unto thee; they shall sing thy name. Selah.
 
1. Shout unto God, all the earth The psalm begins with this general declaration, which is afterwards reduced to particulars.
“Generalis est praefatio, quam mox sequentur hypotheses.” — Lat. “C’est une preface generale, dont les applications speciales suivent incontinent apres.” — Fr.
He addresses himself to the whole world, and from this it would seem evident, that he predicts the extent to which the kingdom of God should reach at the coming of Christ. In the second verse the call is repeated with increasing vehemency, to stir up to the praises of God, such as might otherwise be remiss in the service. To sing the honor of his name, is an expression sufficiently obvious; meaning, that we should extol his sacred name in a manner suitable to its dignity, so that it may obtain its due and deserved adoration. But the clause which follows is rather ambiguous. Some think that it conveys a repetition of the same idea contained in other words, and read, set forth the glory of his praise.
Hammond’s objection to this is, that if כבור, glory, were in the construct state, governing the noun which follows, and giving this reading, the glory of his, praise, the vowel should be changed from kamets, to segol
I prefer taking the Hebrew word signifying praise to be in the accusative case; rendering the words literally, make a glory his praise. And by this I understand him to mean, not as some do, that we should glory exclusively in his praises,
This is Aben Ezra’s view. He would read, “Make your glory his praise;” that is, let it be your glory to praise him.
but simply, that we highly exalt his praises, that they may be glorious. The Psalmist is not satisfied with our declaring them moderately, and insists that we should celebrate his goodness in some measure proportionably to its excellence.
